name: Saudi Arabia
summary_text: Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under its uncodified Sharia legal system, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and the morality police enforce with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned. Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a Pakistani trans woman died in custody in Riyadh in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. Amnesty International reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the Kingdom — and device inspection at the border is an established risk. The tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia LGBTQ Laws: Penalties and Visitor Rules - LegalClarity
sources.claim_summary: LegalClarity overview (June 2026): Saudi Arabia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity - flogging, lengthy imprisonment and in the most severe cases death; no codified penal code (judges apply their own interpretation of Islamic law under the Basic Law of Governance); no protections, no relationship recognition, no gender-transition pathway; explains how the system works without a penal code and what visitors need to know.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): penalties based on Shariah with a maximum punishment of death; people suspected of homosexuality and trans women have been arrested, detained, tortured and prosecuted on morality grounds ('cross-dressing', 'offenses against Islam', 'attacks against public morals'); known executions for same-sex intimacy usually involve additional charges; in 2019 the state security agency published a video categorising feminism and homosexuality as 'extremist ideas' punishable by prison and flogging.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 country review of Saudi Arabia: deviation from traditional gender norms is a criminal offence under Sharia (social behaviour, medical interventions, surgical transition); no explicit legislation but arrests and severe punishments including corporal retribution are common; gender-affirming healthcare permitted only for intersex people; the Permanent Committee for Islamic Research rejects gender-affirming care and suggests prayer for gender dysphoria.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex activity illegal with capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging, fines and deportation; no gender-identity recognition; sections on enforcement cases, censorship, living conditions, and HIV/AIDS (including treatment of foreigners).

sources.title: The transgender tailor who died in Saudi custody - BBC News
sources.claim_summary: BBC (May 2017): the transgender tailor who died in Saudi custody - Pakistani trans elder Mohammad Amin ('Meeno Baji') was arrested at a party of transgender Pakistanis in Riyadh, thrown in Azizia prison, and died that night; Pakistani activists say he was beaten with clubs and hosepipes; Saudi authorities said he had a heart attack.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia: 5 arrested for cross-dressing on social media
sources.claim_summary: Gulf News (Oct 2021): five Saudi men arrested for cross-dressing - they filmed themselves walking the streets of the Northern Borders province and posted the video on social media; police said the conduct was 'inconsistent with the public morals of society'; criminal sanctions for cross-dressing mirror those for homosexuality (imprisonment, fines, deportation for foreigners).

sources.title: Visitors to Saudi Arabia imprisoned for social media posts
sources.claim_summary: Amnesty International/ALQST (June 2026, updated July 2026): visitors to Saudi Arabia - including tourists and Hajj/Umrah pilgrims - risk detention, grossly unfair trials and lengthy prison sentences for their social media activity, including posts published before entering the Kingdom; eight documented cases (July 2022 to late 2025), predominantly from Global South and Middle Eastern countries.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia says it welcomes LGBTQ visitors | CNN
sources.claim_summary: CNN Travel: 'Saudi Arabia says it welcomes LGBTQ visitors' — Saudi tourism authorities tell LGBTQ travellers they are welcome as the kingdom courts international tourism, though same-sex conduct remains criminalised and visitors are urged to keep a low profile.

sources.title: Safety and security - Saudi Arabia travel advice - GOV.UK
sources.claim_summary: UK FCDO travel advice for Saudi Arabia: advises against all travel to parts and all but essential travel to other parts; safety and security, regional risks, pilgrimage guidance. General travel advice.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ Risk Map - A3M Global Monitoring
sources.claim_summary: A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map 2025 (with Diversity Tourism and ITB Berlin): country dossiers assessing traveller risk on 80+ criteria; a world map assessing safety for LGBTQ+ travellers, with risk levels from 1 (low risk) upward, plus surveys and interviews with travel experts and community travellers.

sources.title: Saudis' tough line on gays | World news | The Guardian
sources.claim_summary: The Guardian (April 2005) by Brian Whitaker: 'Saudis' tough line on gays' - dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and 'behaving like women' at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes plus up to two years' jail, after a closed trial without defence lawyers; HRW's Scott Long: 'Prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct are flagrant human rights violations.'
